extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, translators, and literary critics; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance on poetic diction, translation, metaphor, parody, and general literary style — oriented to writers, translators, and critics assessing poetic and dramatic works. Emphasizes clarity, consistency of imagery, fidelity in translation, and methods of reading and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic construction and detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of Shakespeare is grounded not only in general construction but 'in all the details, of his dramas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic works for coherence at both the macro (overall construction) and micro (detail-level) scales — both plot architecture and the handling of particulars contribute to greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise position and choice of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'the almost faultless position and choice of words, in Pope’s original compositions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and aim for exactness in diction and word order; felicitous placement of words creates clarity and aesthetic effect. Use sentence-level analysis (word-by-word) when critiquing diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corrupting poetic diction in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that Pope’s translation of Homer became 'the main source of our pseudo-poetic diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators should avoid introducing artificial or mannered phrasing that corrupts readers' taste; beware of translations that create a false poetic idiom in the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective sense over isolated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of readers who take pleasure 'from the separate images and phrases successively, without asking themselves whether the collective meaning was sense or nonsense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or crafting poetry, ensure that attractive individual lines/images cohere into a sensible and meaningful whole rather than merely producing isolated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice sense for elevated diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between a just image ('the stars ... shine pre-eminently bright') and lines where 'the sense or the diction be the more absurd.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High or ornate diction must still convey clear sense; elevated words should not mask nonsensical or incoherent meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of re-examination and critical correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal account of being induced 'to re-examine with impartial strictness Gray’s celebrated Elegy,' discovering defects but gaining greater delight in the remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and readers should re-evaluate admired works critically; acknowledging faults can lead to deeper appreciation and improved craft through revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in metaphors and similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Example where 'the Dog Star ... is turned into a real dog' and 'the whole visual likeness is lost,' showing how mixed or exaggerated imagery ruins the simile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent frame of reference in comparisons; ensure the visual and the conceptual elements of a simile or metaphor align, avoiding absurd or mixed metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and visual puns must be justifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense that in Spenser and Fletcher 'the thought is justifiable; for the images are at least consistent, and it was the intention of the writers to mark the seasons by this allegory of visualized puns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of allegory, visual puns, and emblematic imagery should be intentional and coherent with the poem's aims; contextualize such devices so they don't appear arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on personal malignity or gossip in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of an 'age of personality' where 'the most vapid satires' gain interest solely because they name contemporaries and encourage gossip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should target ideas and behaviors, not trade on personal scandal; avoid gratuitous identification of contemporaries or vindictive asides that substitute gossip for artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not tell only half the facts (avoid deceptive omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: One instance 'of deception, by the telling the half of a fact, and omitting the other half' producing a false impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and countervailing facts matter; in criticism and narrative, present sufficient context to avoid misleading readers by selective omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance components when making broad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: On Dryden’s line 'Great wit ... to madness sure is near allied' the author notes genius comprises multiple components that must be balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sweeping generalizations based on a single trait; evaluate complex qualities (e.g., genius) by considering all relevant components and how they modify one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce work that engages rather than anesthetizes readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal of 'devotees of the circulating libraries' whose reading is 'a sort of beggarly day-dreaming' supplied by printed phantasms rather than productive thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to create writing that provokes thought and reflection rather than encouraging passive, vapid consumption; value substance and intellectual engagement in literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill in selection, translation, and arrangement (compilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that a compilation 'uniting the charms of romance and history, keeps the imagination so constantly on the wing, and yet leaves so much for after reflection' requires great genius in 'translation, selection, and arrangement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and compilers should exercise discriminating taste in choosing, ordering, and translating material so as to balance imaginative stimulation with space for reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody must blend likeness with difference (avoid mere silliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that to ridicule a silly poem by writing 'another still sillier' only proves the parodist 'a still greater blockhead'; 'a just imitation' requires a balancing difference with the likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective parody captures the original's characteristics while introducing critical distance or insight; avoid crude mimicry that simply amplifies the target's faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of construction; avoid harsh or obscure syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Example of Wordsworth's early lines exhibiting 'harsh and obscure construction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor sentence constructions that convey meaning clearly; watch for awkward inversions or opaque phrasing that impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain precise semantic distinctions to prevent equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'two distinct meanings are confounded under one or more words ... erroneous consequences will be drawn' — remedy by substituting or appropriating distinct words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in vocabulary choice; where a single term has multiple senses, clarify or coin/appropriate terms to avoid misleading generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for historical shifts in 'common sense' and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Common sense, therefore, differs in different ages' — terms and what is 'evident to common sense' change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret and use terms with awareness of their historical and cultural meanings; what seems obvious in one era may be contentious in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'idea' (abstract) from 'image' (sensuous) and use philosophical terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the word 'idea' in Plato, Locke, Hume: idea as visual abstraction vs impression; warning about vague uses causing error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deploying philosophical or abstract vocabulary in writing, define/clarify the sense intended to avoid confusion between mental images and abstract concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose vocabulary to preserve harmony of words and logical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification for using the word 'intensify' to preserve 'that harmony of the position of the words with the logical position of the thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words not only for meaning but for their fit in the sentence's rhythmic and logical architecture; coin or adopt words sparingly when they preserve compositional harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and render idiomatic language by associating words with objects and speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice for acquiring a language: 'learning all the words, that could possibly be so learned, with the objects before me' and 'ask the mother in the house, the children ... the common man on the market.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators and writers seeking authentic speech should learn vocabulary in situ and from native speakers, privileging living usage over bookish equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural images to heighten elevated or religious feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that when 'the feelings are wrought above the natural pitch by the belief of something mysterious, while all the images are purely natural,' religion and poetry strike deepest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey deep or religious sentiment, pair elevated feeling with concrete, natural imagery rather than contrived or hyperbolic images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject (discursive vs intuitive modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: 'Philosophy has hitherto been discursive; while Geometry is always and essentially intuitive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate mode of exposition for the subject matter: use discursive argument where analysis is required and intuitive presentation where direct apprehension is primary.
